items: Goose is a memory-safe systems language, and this is the quick tour.
In about five minutes: what it is, how it builds, and how it treats memory.
Who here has fought a borrow checker or tuned a garbage collector?
The room knows this is a short, high-level tour.
tips: Where it comes from
Goose SDK v2026.4. Docs: ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/ (start with index.md and tutorial.md).

items: Goose is a systems language for fast programs that cannot corrupt memory.
Three points: it runs like C, it has no garbage collector, and it is safe by default.
The hello program: one function, one print.
Fast like C, no GC, safe by default.
tips: If asked about syntax
It reads like C or Rust: statically typed, with inference, in .goose files. See ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/tutorial.md.
If asked how run is instant
goose run compiles in memory with the bundled TinyCC; goose build hands the C to the system compiler (clang). See ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/command_line.md.

items: The first box: your source file, app.goose.
You write ordinary Goose code in a .goose file.
An arrow to the second box: one C file.
Goose turns all your code into a single C file.
tips: For detail questions
The compiler stages are covered in ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/implementation.md; keep them for the longer talk.

items: The last arrow lands on your program.
A C compiler does the rest, so you get a native, fast program.
Goose compiles to C and gets out of the way.
tips: Run versus build
goose run uses the bundled TinyCC for instant runs; goose build uses clang or another system C compiler for an optimized binary.

items: The left panel: most languages have a stack and a heap.
The heap needs a garbage collector, or you free memory by hand.
The right panel starts as the same picture.
The first column: cheap to allocate.
New data goes on top of the stack, like stacking plates.
The second column: cleanup is automatic.
When a block ends, its memory is gone. No collector, no pauses.
The third column: data stays put.
Values never move, so references to them stay valid.
No heap means simpler memory, faster programs, and no pauses.
The top row: null and bounds.
If a value can be missing, you have to check it.
tips: If asked about nullable values
Missing values are written T?, and the compiler makes you handle the empty case.
If asked about speed
The optimizer removes many bounds checks it can prove safe (bounds-check elimination).

items: The bottom row: dangling references and data races.
A reference cannot outlive the data it points to.
Threads do not share memory; they pass messages.
The compiler catches these before your program ever runs.
tips: If asked about threads
Threads communicate with queues instead of shared state. See ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/goose_spec.md.

items: Speed and memory against C++ and Rust, from the public Goose benchmarks.
The left card is how much better Goose is: above 1x means Goose wins.

items: The right card: memory for 16 million records. Everyday C++ is 713 MB.
Idiomatic C++ is the baseline here.
Expert C++ gets down to 557 MB. Notice the bar above shrinks to keep the scale fair.
Safe Rust lands at 593 MB, in the same neighbourhood.
Goose does it in 149 MB. Watch how everything else stretches to keep the scale honest.
So I wondered: fast language, fast web server? I built one and measured it.
Left, a todo API under load. Right, a shop site.
tips: Where the numbers come from
The user's own goose-bench results, one worker each on the same machine.

items: Flask, a typical Python server, tops out around 2.5 thousand requests a second.
Express handles about 59 thousand, and Flask is squashed against the floor.
Goose reaches about 178 thousand, three times Express. Everything else shrinks again.
Next.js, a popular JavaScript framework, serves 13.6 thousand requests a second.
Goose serves 223 thousand requests a second, about sixteen times more.
Production Node runs more workers, so the gap shrinks on a bigger box. This is one worker each.
Memory at rest: Next.js sits at 105 MB.
Next.js takes 267 ms to serve the first page.
A fast language gives you a fast, tiny web server.

tips: For detail questions
Goose uses data stacks with a bump pointer: allocating moves a pointer, leaving a block resets it. See ~/Documents/goose/goose-sdk/goose-v2026.4-macos-arm64/docs/goose_spec.md.
